mainEntity.name: How much does an Audi A7 30 TDI / 45 TDI / 50 TDI engine replacement cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: A full reconditioned or rebuilt Audi A7 30 TDI / 45 TDI / 50 TDI engine typically costs between £2,800 and £8,000 for the supply-only unit, depending on whether it is the 2.0L four-cylinder or the 3.0L V6 variant. Used engines start from around £1,200. Fully rebuilt units with upgraded components and a 12-month warranty sit at the higher end of the scale. Supply and fit labour will add approximately £650-£1,040 depending on the specialist.

mainEntity.name: What are the signs of turbocharger oil strainer failure in an Audi A7 30 TDI / 45 TDI / 50 TDI?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most common early warning sign is a distinct whining noise from the turbocharger or a loss of power under acceleration. You may also notice the engine management light illuminating. In severe cases, oil starvation can cause a knocking sound from the bottom end. Ignoring these signs can lead to rapid catastrophic internal engine damage.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine in an Audi A7 30 TDI / 45 TDI / 50 TDI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if the vehicle is in good overall condition, a reconditioned engine replacement is a financially sound decision that restores reliability. Typical C8 generation Audi A7 30 TDI / 45 TDI / 50 TDI models are valued between £22,000 and £50,000, making a £3,500-£6,000 rebuilt engine a small fraction of the car's worth. For older C7 models valued under £8,000, a high-quality used engine swap may offer a better return on investment.

mainEntity.name: How long does an Audi A7 30 TDI / 45 TDI / 50 TDI engine replacement take?

acceptedAnswer.text: A straightforward supply and fit of a reconditioned Audi A7 30 TDI / 45 TDI / 50 TDI engine typically takes 2 to 3 days at a specialist workshop. This timeframe includes draining fluids, removing the old unit, and installing the replacement. Necessary ECU adaptations, AdBlue system recalibration, and road testing are completed before handover. Complex cases involving additional damage may extend this timeframe.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between the 2.0L and 3.0L V6 diesel engines in the Audi A7 30 TDI / 45 TDI / 50 TDI?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 2.0L variant (CLZB) produces 204hp and prioritises fuel efficiency and lower tax bands, often badged as 40 TDI but grouped in the lower-tier diesel bracket. The 3.0L V6 variants (CDUD/CRTD at 245-286hp) utilise the EA897 architecture, offering superior refinement, stronger mid-range torque, and standard quattro all-wheel drive. Both benefit from mild-hybrid technology in the C8 generation, but the V6 requires more rigorous adherence to AdBlue and oil service intervals.

historyTimeline.h2: Audi A7 30 TDI / 45 TDI / 50 TDI - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: When the diesel variants of the A7 Sportback launched, they offered a potent, efficient alternative to petrol, evolving from the early 3.0 TDI V6 units to the modern mild-hybrid 45 TDI and 50 TDI architectures, alongside the highly efficient 2.0L four-cylinder.

milestones.description: CDUC / CDUD (3.0L V6 TDI, 204-245hp) introduced in the C7 generation, establishing the A7 as a capable grand tourer with strong torque and quattro capability.
CRTD (3.0L V6 TDI, 245hp) launched with the C7 facelift, featuring Euro 6 compliance and revised emissions systems to meet stricter environmental standards.
CLZB (2.0L TDI, 204hp) and updated 3.0L V6 units launched in the C8 generation, incorporating 12V/48V mild-hybrid (MHEV) technology for enhanced efficiency and refined power delivery.

problems.group: AdBlue / SCR System & EGR Cooler Leaks
problems.h4: AdBlue / SCR System & EGR Cooler Leaks - Why the Audi A7 30 TDI / 45 TDI / 50 TDI (CLZB/CRTD) Cooling System Fails
problems.affectedModels: Audi A7 30 TDI / 45 TDI / 50 TDI (CLZB, CRTD, 2015-present)
problems.rootCause: The AdBlue heater element or dosing injector can fail, leading to crystallisation and "Start prohibited" warnings. Similarly, the EGR cooler internal matrix can degrade, allowing coolant to mix with exhaust gases or leak externally.

repairOptions.longevity: Highly effective; resolves the root cause permanently if caught before severe overheating.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply & fit, upgraded components addressing the original failure point, 12-month warranty.
repairOptions.longevity: Only necessary if coolant loss was ignored, resulting in severe overheating, warped cylinder heads, or hydrostatic lock.

A reconditioned engine at £3,500-£6,000 remains a highly viable investment to protect the vehicle's retained value. problems.recommendation: Monitor coolant levels and AdBlue warnings religiously. Replace the EGR cooler preventatively if leaks are detected. If the engine has overheated, do not attempt a cheap repair; opt for a reconditioned engine with a warranty to avoid recurring issues.
